# Deuteronomy 20 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

Deuteronomy 20 contains Israel's laws of warfare, covering three main sections: (a) pre-battle exhortation and exemptions (vv. 1–9), (b) rules for besieging cities — distant cities versus Canaanite cities (vv. 10–18), and (c) preservation of fruit trees during siege (vv. 19–20). The chapter is the only legislation in the Torah devoted entirely to the conduct of war (Precept Austin, citing Coates / Moody Bible Commentary).

---

## v. 1 — The Command to Trust God, Not Fear Superior Forces

**Traditional reading:** Moses commands Israel not to fear even when the enemy has superior horses, chariots, and numbers. "Do not be afraid" (the Hebrew verb in the Qal imperfect) is a recurring theme in holy war contexts (cf. Deut 1:21, 29; 3:2, 22; 7:18; 31:6, 8). Israel was to fear YHWH, not the enemy (Precept Austin, citing Utley). The ground of confidence is twofold: (1) "the LORD your God is with you," and (2) He already proved Himself by bringing Israel out of Egypt. This is not blind trust but trust based on past evidence of God's power (Enduring Word). Calvin says this law "is a Supplement to the First Commandment, enacting that they should carry on their wars under the auspices of God" — they were not to rest their hopes on anything but invocation of His name (Calvin, StudyLight.org). Gill notes the Targum of Jonathan adds: "for His Word shall be your help," identifying the eternal Logos as Israel's help. Ellicott observes that the Israelite army was entirely infantry while enemies had cavalry and chariots; most great victories were won without these.

## v. 2 — The Priest Addresses the Army

**Traditional reading:** As battle draws near, a priest — not just any priest, but one specifically appointed and (according to Jewish tradition) anointed for war, called *mashuach milchamah* ("the anointed of war") — comes forward. Gill cites Maimonides describing this priest being anointed with the anointing oil specifically for this role. Ellicott notes there is no mention of the Levite here; the priest is a distinct personage whose words constitute "the blessing of Jehovah on the campaign," implying Israel could not lawfully go to war except when Jehovah's blessing could be invoked. The NET Bible note (cited in Precept Austin) suggests the reference to the priest implies also the presence of the ark of the covenant, the visible sign of God's presence, marking this as "holy war" or "Yahweh war." The IVP Bible Background Commentary notes that Assyrian texts and reliefs similarly depict priests accompanying troops, carrying images of the gods, performing rituals, and addressing the army.

## v. 3 — "Do Not Be Fainthearted or Afraid"

**Traditional reading:** The priest's speech is a fourfold prohibition against fear: "do not let your heart faint," "do not be afraid," "do not tremble" (or "make haste" / panic), and "do not be terrified." Gill, citing the Mishnah (Sotah 8:1), explains each phrase corresponds to a specific military intimidation tactic used by enemy kings: (1) heart-fainting at the neighing of horses and brightness of swords, (2) fear at the clashing of shields, (3) trembling at the sound of trumpets, (4) terror at the voice of shouting. Calvin remarks that God "forbids their fears not in one word only, but heaps many together," showing "how difficult it is to cure that evil — fear, which in so many different ways assails and disturbs our minds." Ellicott notes that Isaiah used similar language to strengthen Ahaz (Isa 7:4): "fear not, neither be faint-hearted."

## v. 4 — "The LORD Your God Goes With You to Fight for You"

**Traditional reading:** The reason for courage: God Himself goes with the army to fight and give victory. Ellicott quotes Rashi: "They come in the might of flesh and blood; but ye come in the might of the Eternal." The verse is echoed in David's words to Goliath (1 Sam 17:45) and Psalm 20:7: "Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will remember the name of the LORD our God." Precept Austin notes that according to the Mishnah (Sotah 8:1), this statement "respects the ark" — the visible symbol of the Divine Presence that accompanied Israel into battle (cf. Josh 6:4). Enduring Word applies this spiritually: the believer today should look to Jesus Christ, the High Priest and captain of salvation (Heb 2:10; 4:14–16), for encouragement in spiritual warfare.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/20.htm

## v. 5 — Exemption: The Man Who Built a New House

**Traditional reading:** The officers (*shoterim* — civil magistrates or genealogical record-keepers, per Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary) announce that anyone who built a new house but has not "dedicated" it may return home. "Dedicated" (Hebrew *chanak*) does not mean consecration to holy use as with the temple, but a formal ceremony of taking possession — probably festive, with friends gathered for a celebration (Gill). Merrill (cited in Enduring Word) notes the verb is used for Solomon's dedication of the temple (1 Kgs 8:63) and the walls of Jerusalem (Neh 12:27), carrying "strong religious overtones, suggesting that what was being done was a sacred ceremony before the Lord." Josephus (cited in the Pulpit Commentary) says this exemption lasted one year, analogous to Deuteronomy 24:5. The rationale is both compassionate — it would be a hardship for a man to die before enjoying his new home — and practical: a soldier distracted by unfinished business at home would not fight wholeheartedly (Enduring Word).

## v. 6 — Exemption: The Man Who Planted a Vineyard

**Traditional reading:** A man who planted a vineyard but has not yet "eaten of it" (literally, "made it common" or "profaned it" — i.e., begun to use its fruit for ordinary consumption) is exempt. The Pulpit Commentary explains that trees planted for food could not be used before the fifth year under Leviticus 19:23–25 (three years uncircumcised, fourth year holy to the LORD, fifth year for common eating). Gill notes the Targums of Jerusalem and Jonathan interpret "not eaten of it" in light of this law. The same compassion-and-focus principle applies as in v. 5.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/20.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/20.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-20/

## v. 7 — Exemption: The Betrothed Man

**Traditional reading:** A man betrothed but not yet married is exempt. Betrothal in ancient Israel was a binding covenant, and the man who died in battle would lose his bride to another — a particularly poignant hardship. The Pulpit Commentary places this alongside the house and vineyard exemptions as a domestic consideration that would distract a soldier's heart from battle.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/20.htm
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/20.htm

## v. 8 — Exemption: The Fearful and Fainthearted

**Traditional reading:** The officers add a fourth exemption: the fearful and fainthearted. Two rabbinic interpretations are recorded in the Mishnah (Sotah 8:5, cited by Gill): Rabbi Akiba says this refers to a man who cannot stand in battle array or behold a drawn sword. Rabbi Jose the Galilean says it refers to one who is afraid because of his sins — the Targum of Jonathan adds "because of his sin." The law strategically links this exemption to the three previous ones (house, vineyard, betrothal) so that a man could return home on one of those pretexts without the public shame of being identified as a coward (Gill). The stated reason: "lest the hearts of his brothers melt like his own" — fear is contagious, and one coward can undermine the morale of an entire unit (Enduring Word). Gideon's reduction of his army from 32,000 to 10,000 by sending home the fearful (Judg 7:3) is the only recorded instance of this rule being applied (Ellicott).

- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/20.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/20.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-20/

## v. 9 — Appointment of Commanders

**Traditional reading:** After the exemptions are declared and those men depart, captains (*sarim*) are appointed over the remaining troops. Ellicott notes these were "special leaders for the campaigns, whose command would probably cease when it was over." The Pulpit Commentary clarifies that while *sar tsava* (captain of a host) usually designates the commander-in-chief, here the plural refers to chiefs of companies or detachments. Enduring Word observes that trust in God did not eliminate the need for good human leadership. A Jewish tradition (cited in Gill) says the officers stationed "stout men" before the army and behind them with iron hatchets to cut off the legs of any who tried to flee.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/20.htm

## v. 10 — Offer of Peace to Distant Cities

**Traditional reading:** Before attacking a city, Israel must first "proclaim peace unto it" — i.e., offer terms of surrender. This applies to cities "far away," outside the seven Canaanite nations (see v. 15). Gill, citing Maimonides and Jarchi, notes this concerns "arbitrary" (voluntary) war, not the commanded conquest of Canaan. Calvin regards this as evidence "that, even in lawful wars, cruelty is to be repressed, and bloodshed to be abstained from as much as possible." He notes that even pagan nations recognized this principle through the institution of heralds and formal declarations of war. Ellicott contrasts this with the Danites who massacred Laish without warning (Judg 18:27–28).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/deuteronomy-20.html

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/20.htm

## v. 11 — Terms of Surrender: Tributary Labor

**Traditional reading:** If the city accepts peace and opens its gates, its inhabitants become "forced laborers" (*mas* — tribute service). The Pulpit Commentary explains the Hebrew *mas* denotes service rendered as tribute, whether for a season or perpetually (cf. Gen 49:15; Judg 1:30, 33, 35; 1 Kgs 5:13; 9:21). Gill clarifies this does not mean chattel slavery but a form of vassalage: paying annual tribute and being called upon for public works — as the Moabites, Syrians, and Edomites became servants of David (2 Sam 8:2). The terms of peace, according to Jewish tradition, also required renunciation of idolatry (Gill, citing Jarchi).

- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/20.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/20.htm

## vv. 12–13 — Siege and Death of Males

**Traditional reading:** If a city refuses peace and wages war, Israel is to besiege it. When God delivers it, every male is to be put to the sword. Merrill (cited in Enduring Word) says the death of the males was "not only to induce other cities to a more ready submission to Israel but to prevent future uprising in the city that had just been taken." The Pulpit Commentary notes that only the adult fighting males were slain; women and children were spared (v. 14).

**Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin offers a noteworthy reservation here. He says: "The permission here given seems to confer too great a license … how does God, the Father of mercies, give His sanction to indiscriminate bloodshed?" He answers: "It has already been stated, that more was conceded to the Jews on account of their hardness of heart, than was justly lawful for them. Unquestionably, by the law of charity, even armed men should be spared, if, casting away the sword, they crave for mercy; at any rate it was not lawful to kill any but those who were taken in arms, and sword in hand. This permission, therefore, to slaughter, which is extended to all the males, is far distant from perfection." He sees it as a divine accommodation to Israel's hardness, while still restraining worse cruelty (sparing women and children). This reflects a classic Reformed hermeneutic: the Mosaic civil law contains concessions to human sinfulness that fall short of the perfect moral standard.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/deuteronomy-20.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-20/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/20.htm

## v. 14 — Plunder: Women, Children, Livestock, Spoil

**Traditional reading:** Women, children, livestock, and all movable goods may be taken as plunder. The Pulpit Commentary notes "shalt eat the spoil" means to consume it for one's own maintenance. Enduring Word notes that plunder provided wages for the army and underwrote battle expenses; normally plunder was allowed, though sometimes specifically prohibited (e.g., Jericho, Josh 6:17–19).

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-20/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/20.htm

## v. 15 — These Rules Apply to Distant Cities Only

**Traditional reading:** This verse explicitly limits the preceding rules (vv. 10–14, offering peace and sparing women and children) to cities far away, not belonging to the seven Canaanite nations. Wiersbe (cited in Precept Austin) notes that God gave Israel two different military approaches: one for cities in Canaan (vv. 1–9, 16–18) and another for cities outside Canaan (vv. 10–15).

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-20-commentary
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/20.htm

## vv. 16–18 — Complete Destruction (*Herem*) of the Canaanite Nations

**Traditional reading:** For the cities of the Canaanite nations (Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, Jebusites — the Girgashites are omitted, as also in Josh 9:1, perhaps because they accepted peace or fled, per Jewish tradition cited by Gill), nothing that breathes is to be left alive. They are to be "utterly destroyed" (Hebrew *charam* — devoted to destruction). The reason is explicitly stated in v. 18: "so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods, and so cause you to sin against the LORD your God." Enduring Word explains this was "a unique war of judgment, more than a war of conquest or defense" — the Canaanite culture was so morally and spiritually corrupt that God considered it irredeemable and ripe for judgment. Gill notes the capital crimes of the Canaanites included idolatry, incest, witchcraft, soothsaying, and necromancy (see Lev 18:3, 24–28).

**Debate on whether peace was offered:** Some Jewish writers (cited by Gill, referencing Jerusalem Talmud Shebiith and Debarim Rabba) held that Joshua sent three letters into Canaan before entry: one offering the chance to flee, a second offering peace (on condition of becoming proselytes), and a third declaring war. The Girgashites reportedly fled to Africa; the Gibeonites made peace; thirty-one kings made war and fell. Adam Clarke (cited in Enduring Word) suggests "utterly destroy" should be understood as "utterly subdue — slaying them if they resist … or totally expel them from the land, or reduce them to a state of slavery." He uses the examples of Rahab and the Gibeonites to argue Israel did not believe they were bound to kill every individual Canaanite. However, the plain reading of the text ("you shall not leave alive anything that breathes") strongly supports total destruction.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-20/
- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/20.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/20.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/20.htm

## v. 19 — Do Not Destroy Fruit-Bearing Trees During a Siege

**Traditional reading:** During a prolonged siege, Israel is forbidden to cut down fruit-bearing trees for siege works. The rationale: "you can eat their fruit" — these trees sustain human life. The difficult Hebrew phrase literally reads something like "for the man is a tree of the field" or "for the tree of the field is man's life." The Pulpit Commentary discusses the textual problem at length: as the words stand in the Hebrew text, they yield no good sense. The ancient solutions include: (1) reading it interrogatively (LXX, Rashi): "Is the tree of the field a man, that it should come into siege before you?" — i.e., the tree is not an enemy combatant that can flee or fight, so why cut it down? (2) reading as a negation (Targum of Onkelos, Vulgate): "For the tree of the field is not a man to come into siege before you." Ellicott favours the interrogative reading. Enduring Word emphasises the ecological wisdom: God required Israel to take a long-term view and not win at any cost. Clarke says: "It was a merciful provision to spare all fruit-bearing trees, because they yielded the fruit which supported man's life; and it was sound policy also, for even the conquerors must perish if the means of life were cut off."

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/20.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/20.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-20/

## v. 20 — Non-Fruit-Bearing Trees May Be Cut for Siege Works

**Traditional reading:** Trees that do not bear food may be cut down for constructing siege works (bulwarks, battering rams, towers) against the resisting city until it falls. The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary (from search excerpt) notes: "It is evident that some sort of military engines were intended; and accordingly we know, that in Egypt, where the Israelites learned their military tactics, the method of conducting a siege was by throwing up banks, and making advances with movable towers, or with the testudo [Wilkinson]." Enduring Word observes that this command is "another example of how God did not allow Israel to conduct total war or win a battle at any cost."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-20/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/deuteronomy-20.html (from search excerpt)

## Points of Difference Among Protestant Traditions

**Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin's commentary (StudyLight.org / CCEL) provides the most distinctive traditional voice available. He reads the chapter through the lens of the First Commandment — war must be conducted under God's auspices. Most notably, on vv. 12–13, Calvin explicitly states that the command to kill all males in a resisting city "is far distant from perfection" and was a concession to Israel's hardness of heart, reflecting the Reformed hermeneutic that the Mosaic civil law contains accommodations that fall short of the moral law. He also emphasizes that Israel could not lawfully go to war except when God's blessing could be invoked (v. 2).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/deuteronomy-20.html
- https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment2/v1.0/harry/comm_vol04/htm/ii.x.xi.htm

**Evangelical / broadly Pentecostal (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik's commentary treats the passage as spiritually applicable to believers today — the priest prefigures Christ our High Priest, the exemptions teach that God wants willing and committed soldiers, and the conquest of Canaan is a unique war of judgment, not a model for all warfare. The focus is on faith, courage, and wholehearted commitment.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-20/

**Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, Anglican:** Specific commentaries from these traditions on Deuteronomy 20 were not located in the searches performed. DesiringGod.org, GTY.org, LCMS.org, 1517.org, Seedbed.com, and Wesley.nnu.edu did not yield results for Deuteronomy 20 verse-by-verse commentary in the available search results. Spurgeon's Verse Expositions lists the chapter but no detailed content was retrievable.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/deuteronomy.html

## Other Views

**Jewish Tradition (via Gill and Ellicott):** The rabbinic concept of the "anointed of war" (*mashuach milchamah*) is extensively discussed. Maimonides describes two addresses by this priest: one at muster (about exemptions), and one at the battle line ("fear not"). The Mishnah (Sotah 8) connects the four fear-terms of v. 3 to specific enemy intimidation tactics. The debate between R. Akiba and R. Jose on the meaning of "fearful and fainthearted" (physical cowardice vs. fear due to sin) is preserved. The tradition that the Girgashites fled to Africa and that Joshua sent three letters (flee, make peace, or fight) is recorded in the Jerusalem Talmud.

- https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/20.htm
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/20.htm

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes):** The NET note (cited in Precept Austin) emphasises that the reference to the priest "suggests also the presence of the ark of the covenant" and that the whole setting reflects "holy war" or "Yahweh war," in which God Himself takes the initiative as true commander of Israel's forces.

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-20-commentary

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** Specific commentaries from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org on Deuteronomy 20 were not located in the searches performed. The Vulgate's reading of v. 19 (treating the difficult Hebrew phrase as a negation: "for the tree of the field is not a man") is noted by the Pulpit Commentary.

- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/deuteronomy/20.htm

**Morgan's Exposition (G. Campbell Morgan):** Views the Canaanite war as God's scourge against a "corrupt and corrupting people." The army sifting ensures only wholehearted men fight. The offer of peace to distant cities and sparing of fruit trees are "remarkable evidences of the divine attention to the smallest matters."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gcm/deuteronomy-20.html (from search excerpt)
